anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly + CPU Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level statement or transaction design forces the engine to read, join, or hold more data than the business requirement actually needs.
Database Configuration Parameter Anomaly : Instance-level settings for memory, parallelism, logging, and background workers are mis-tuned relative to hardware capacity and workload characteristics.
CPU Resource Anomaly : Host CPU cores are saturated by database processes, throttling all other work even if other resources are still available.

When these three root causes coexist, symptoms from each layer amplify one another: long-running or chatty queries generated by the workload logic push large volumes of work into the executor; mis-sized work-memory, buffer, and parallelism parameters force the engine either to spill, over-parallelize, or repeatedly flush checkpoints, creating bursts of CPU demand that drive core utilization to sustained saturation. Observable phenomena therefore include: a slow-query log crowded with the same expensive statements, CPU wait events dominating wait-class views, run-queue lengths spiking during checkpoints or sort/hash phases, sudden latency cliffs whenever statement concurrency rises, and apparent hardware under-utilization of I/O or network despite high end-to-end response times.

Causally, inefficient workload logic is the initial generator of excessive CPU instructions and memory pressure. Mis-tuned configuration parameters remove the safety valves that could have absorbed or mitigated that pressure—e.g., too little work memory forces repetitive in-memory operations, while excessive parallelism multiplies the CPU footprint of each bad plan. The compounding effect drives the system into true CPU saturation, which in turn lengthens query runtimes, keeping transactions open longer and further increasing concurrency and memory churn. The feedback loop masks the individual contribution of each root cause, making the overall anomaly harder to diagnose and capable of crippling both transactional and analytical workloads.

entry.official_description: Could not open file '%s' for error logging%s%s
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with file creation, filesystem access, write durability, log persistence, tablespace management, or storage-capacity boundaries.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect filesystem capacity and permissions, verify persistence paths, review log and data placement, and check whether storage latency or write failures are affecting the engine.
